content.thinking:
I'm setting up the loft dimensions along section axes, then starting the code draft with imports for the builder and frame/line utilities, keeping colors limited to a snapped palette.

Now I'm defining the fur, cream, bark, and leaf color ramps, then writing a cellPaint function for fur shading that varies brightness with surface normal and noise, plus a cream-colored chest/belly patch based on normal direction and vertical position.

I'm also adding a speckled rump patch near the back-bottom using normal and position checks plus random brown dots, and setting a dither cell size for the gradient look. Now I'm laying out the skeleton joint coordinates, starting with root and hips and building the spine chain upward with named joints.

Continuing upward, I'm adding the neck chain parented to the chest tip joint, then placing the head joint with a forward-aimed direction vector.

For the head, I'm defining its local coordinate frame relative to the neck and computing a head center point, then starting to build the skull as a scaled sphere mesh attached to the head bone.

Now I'm positioning the muzzle and nose as smaller scaled spheres offset forward and slightly down from the head center, working out z-depth values so the nose bridge sits properly in front of the muzzle, which sits in front of the skull.

Then I'm calculating eye placement by finding points on the skull sphere's surface using the ellipsoid equation, so the eye decals sit flush against the curved front of the head with correct direction vectors for projection.

Thinking through eye texture design -- a dark ring with a small white highlight to give a glossy look, deciding to skip any lighter brow patch since koalas don't really have one.

Now placing the ears near the top of the head, working out their outward-facing position and orientation relative to the skull.

Shaping each ear's outline using a stepped silhouette that approximates a rounded circle, then extruding it into 3D along the ear's width and height axes.

Working out the cross product so x×y equals d, then placing the ear's bottom-center anchor and adding a slightly offset front plate plus a fur tuft ring around it.

For the rim tufts, I'll use a ring of cards along the ear's edge line with facing set radially outward and flow oriented toward the ear's normal direction, leaning the tips forward so they flatten naturally onto the surface.

Now I'm working out the ear and jaw skeleton: ears get their own hinge joints parented to the head, and the jaw gets a joint placed under the skull that pivots forward, with a small cream-colored sphere forming the lower jaw and chin, plus a dark slab underneath to suggest the mouth interior.

I'm also adding cheek fur tufts scattered along the sides of the skull using filtered surface sampling, then moving on to the arms -- setting up the left shoulder joint and figuring out a branch path for the hand grip point using interpolated coordinates.

Now I'm computing the limb for the arm, aiming the wrist toward the branch grip point offset outward by the branch radius, then wrapping the fingers around the branch using the local tangent frame at that point.

Building finger chains with three joints each, then sweeping the geometry along each chain with tapered radii and round caps, plus a claw spike at the tip of each digit.

Working out the palm bar as a gripping pad with darker underside coloring, then thinking through the koala forepaw's digit arrangement—three fingers opposed against two thumb-like digits gripping from the opposite side, trying out axial offset spacings for each digit.

I need to work out the arc direction using the right-hand rule about the wrap axis, checking the cross product sign to determine which way the fingers curl around the front. Computing the arc length, 200° at radius 0.05 gives 0.17, way too long for a stylized koala finger—so I'll scale back to around 100-110° to match a realistic ~0.09 digit length.

Fingers wrap 110° forward while thumbs wrap 90° the opposite way, with the grip radius set at 0.038-0.04 to keep the arm from intersecting the branch. Now I'm working out the leg placement—hip joints at (±0.115, 0.655, -0.03) and finding where the hind foot grips the branch by locating the closest point along the branch curve near y=0.62.

Since the foot target ends up very close to the hip, the limb has to fold sharply, which pushes the knee far forward to compensate for the short distance.

Let me pull the foot grip point farther along the branch instead, maybe around 0.2 away from the hip, so the thigh and shin stretch more naturally and bend only moderately. I'll check that the hand and foot grips stay reasonably spaced apart along the branch so the pose doesn't look cramped.

Checking the shoulder-to-hand distance, the arm needs to stretch out with a slight elbow droop to reach the branch comfortably, angled down and back a bit. The bigger issue now is whether the V-shaped branch spread is wide enough for the koala's shoulder width without forcing an awkward spread-eagle stance.

The head clears both branches with room for the ears, and the torso fits the gap fine. For finishing touches on the display stand, I'm planning pixel-wood base plinths, a small brass-style plaque with "KOALA" lettered in a blocky pixel font, and corner bolt details using tiny sphere shapes.

Adding scene details like moss tufts, fallen leaves, gumnuts, pebbles, and peeling bark strips extruded off the trunk, plus leaf sprays on branch tips using a lanceolate pixel-art leaf texture with a lighter midrib running down the center.

Still shaping leaf curvature...

I'm picking a glaucous blue-green ramp for the eucalypt leaves and planning them as double-sided cards hanging with a downward lean. Sprays at branch tips will scatter small leaf cards along twig points with varied flow, lean, and bend, sized to mimic long koala-browse leaves, aiming for roughly 160 leaf cards in a single textured part with minimal triangle counts per card.

For curled leaf cards I'll use bend segments so each card is built from a small number of triangles, keeping the total count manageable even at a few hundred cards. For the trunk, I'm switching to octagonal sweep sections instead of hexagonal to avoid a blocky look, with cell-painted bark, and adding thin box-section peeling bark ribbons that curl off the trunk along curved paths.

Writing peeling bark ribbons...

Now I'm adding knots as small flattened dark ellipses on the trunk surface, plus base elements: a pixel-textured plank base, moss card clusters scattered on the top slab, and fallen leaf cards laid flat with random orientation across the base.

I'm sizing and layering the base itself — a plinth and top plate with specific heights and footprints, flush with the floor — and sprinkling small brown pixel-textured gumnuts across the base and branches. I'm also planning extra koala surface details like cream chest tufts and fluffy fur outline cards.

For the fur, I'm scattering roughly 150 small tufted cards over the koala's silhouette, tinted with the coat color and distributed across the body, limbs, and head to create a fuzzy pixel-sprinkle look. The tuft texture itself is a small greyscale triangle pattern, tinted lighter with darker edges so it reads as fur when colored by the paint.

Total fur card count comes to about 250 across body and limbs, with 16 triangles each for roughly 4k triangles overall — I still need to add eye details, nose highlight, claws, ear details, and maybe pink toe pads, with darker grey for paw undersides. For the arms, I'm adding a shoulder sphere for extra mass, coloring everything with the shared coat paint for continuity across body, limbs, and head, and placing small eucalyptus leaf clusters near the hands.

Now I'm working out the branch leaf sprays at the tips — skipping the idea of a leaf in the koala's mouth since it stays closed — and designing twigs that curve outward from each branch point using a curved path through a few points, then placing leaf cards at intervals along each twig with an outward flow, collected via a sweep function that walks the path and gathers frames through a callback.

For the leaves themselves, I'm giving them an outward-facing surface with a downward droop to mimic eucalyptus foliage, using a flow vector that points mostly down with some lean and bend variation for naturalism. I'm estimating the total part count stays modest around 200, and adding finishing touches like belly fur and toe pads while deciding to skip a third back branch to keep things simpler.

I'm sketching one more back spray of bark path points curving up behind the koala, checking that the leaves there add depth behind the head without breaking the silhouette too much, and verifying the overall bounding box and floor contact stay sensible for a roughly 1.6m model height.

Now I'm thinking through the hind feet, which share the same five-digit structure as the hands but scaled down, with an opposable big toe lacking a claw, so I can reuse the grip helper. I'm defining a grip function that computes a wrist/foot attachment frame from the branch path and approach direction before building each limb's chain.

I'm defining a branch radius taper function along the path parameter, then mirroring the branch path across the x-axis to generate matching left and right limbs.

Now I'm working out how the branches fork and merge into the trunk, placing a bark-painted knob sphere at the junction so the koala's hips sit slightly embedded into it, then laying out the trunk's curve path points going up through the model.

I'm adding a root flare so the base widens to 0.1 before tapering, and checking whether the branches visually poke through the lower body — deciding that's acceptable since it reads as the branches being tucked behind the fur as the koala sits in the fork.

I'll nudge the branch z-coordinates back to roughly -0.04 so they sit just behind the koala's sides, matching where the hind feet grip, while letting the arms reach slightly forward from the shoulders toward the front.

Checking the geometry at y=0.8, the branch sits outside the body and thigh volume with clear separation, and the foot lands behind the knee near the side of the torso without overlap. I'm now working through the IK for the knee position, tracing from the hip root to the foot target with the offset applied.

The knee ends up displaced forward by about 0.167, placing it ahead of the belly for a natural sitting koala pose with knees poking out slightly. The arms look fine too, going from shoulder to elbow to hand without conflicting with the knee. Now I'm defining spine stations with their z-offsets and widths along the body's loft path to refine the model geometry.

Working out the head joint position in model space, placing the head center so the skull top aligns with overall koala height, and noting the head is proportionally large compared to the body for a cute look. Now I'm ready to start writing the actual mesh-building code, starting with a cell size constant.

Defining fur color ramps and a coat-painting function that uses noise and speckling to vary grey, cream, and brown tones across the surface...

Still working out face and limb coloring logic...

Now I'm sketching the paw colors, eye pixel art pattern with highlights, nose shading, and starting to define the ear shape using row-based outline coordinates.

Still writing ear geometry...

Working out the ear orientation function: facing direction, cross products for x/y axes, and center position, so the thickness axis points forward-out with the front face at positive z, then placing the inner plate slightly offset along that facing direction with a thinner depth.

Adding the tuft ring geometry...

Checking that the ear position overlaps correctly with the skull curvature at that height so the base reads as attached rather than floating. For fur cards, I'll scatter them across the body loft surface, pulling color from the paint layer so the coat tone reads consistently, then work out appropriate texel sizes for the pixel textures versus paint cells.

I'm sizing the tuft texture to roughly 0.0125 per pixel so it reads cleanly at that scale, and then figuring out plank tiling dimensions so the texel size stays consistent across the larger base surface.

For the planks, I'm generating rows with randomized seam offsets to mimic individual boards, then reusing the same texture cropped differently for the side faces so the grain stays consistent across top and sides. Now I'm starting to plan a small brass plaque element to mount on the plinth's front face.

I'm working out the right pixel density and plate dimensions so the engraved text has enough rows to render legibly without making the plaque disproportionately tall, adjusting the texel size down to 0.008 to fit a 37x7 grid.

With the grid sized, I'm applying the whole texture across a thin box as the plaque, then laying out "KOALA" as 3x5 pixel letters with small gaps between them, centered with leaf icons bookending the text, and defining each letter's pixel pattern one row at a time.

For the plaque styling, I'm filling a brass background with a darker border and dark lettering, then mounting it onto the plinth's front face with slight protrusion and tiny bolt details at the corners.

Now I'm writing a plank texture generator that creates wood grain patterns with row-based seams and randomized streaks, building separate dark and light wood palettes for the base materials...

Writing bark paint cells...

Adding twig placement logic...

I'll group all leaf frames into one call with a shared rng for per-card variation, add gumnuts as small brown spheres on the twigs, and randomize leaf spin around the facing axis. For the face I'll use a decal targeting the skull part's surface, and I'm tallying joint counts to confirm the hand/arm/leg digit chains stay within budget.

Now I'm working out the digit chains themselves — each finger built from a short arc path with a tapered radius sweep and round caps, ending in a claw spike attached at the final chain point oriented along the tangent.

For scale, I'm sizing the forepaw like a koala's but chunkier, with digit radius around 0.013, then sketching out a grip function that samples a point and tangent frame along a path at parameter t to position the wrist and fingers for gripping.

input.command: grep -n "  at(\|tangentAt(\|closestT(" src/path.ts | head; grep -n "export function limb" -B2 -A14 src/ik.ts | head -40; grep -n "export function frame\b\|export function line\b" -A6 src/frame.ts | head -30; grep -n "StickOptions\|CardOptions\|DecalOptions" -A25 src/types.ts 2>/dev/null | head -5; ls src
